where: Section 1 (sum of pmf), Section 2 (pattern probability and Y pmf), Section 3 (proof), Exam trap 1, Q1 answer, Q7 answer
problem: Exponents are written without <sup> tags, so the displayed text reads as multiplication. For example '(1 − p)k − 1p', '(1 − p)yp', 'pr − 1(1 − p)k − r', 'P(T > m) = (1 − p)m and P(T > m + n) = (1 − p)m + n; their ratio is (1 − p)n' all say something mathematically false when read literally. A student copying these will get wrong formulas.
fix: Use superscript tags everywhere: P(T = k) = (1 − p)<sup>k − 1</sup>p; P(Y = y) = C(y + r − 1, y) p<sup>r</sup>(1 − p)<sup>y</sup>; pattern probability p<sup>r − 1</sup>(1 − p)<sup>k − r</sup>; P(T > m) = (1 − p)<sup>m</sup>, P(T > m + n) = (1 − p)<sup>m + n</sup>, ratio (1 − p)<sup>n</sup>; and likewise in trap 1, Q1 and Q7.

problem: The summation 'Σk=1∞ (1 − p)k − 1 p = 1' has its limits run together with the summand, which is hard to read on a phone screen.
fix: Write it as Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> (1 − p)<sup>k − 1</sup> p = 1, or in words: the sum over k = 1, 2, 3, ... of (1 − p)<sup>k − 1</sup>p equals 1.

problem: Listed among the uses: 'call-centre arrivals'. Arrivals in a call centre are normally modelled as Poisson counts; the geometric and negative binomial describe waiting for successes in trials, not arrival counts, so the example does not fit the chapter's theme and may mislead.
fix: Either drop call-centre arrivals, or say: counts such as insurance claims or call volumes are modelled as Poisson, and the negative binomial is used instead when those counts are more variable than Poisson allows.
